summary:
Myanmar criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and police enforce it alongside vague public-decency provisions. Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured, while Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas and identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in deaths.

Detention powers reach past Section 377. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment and is applied specifically against transgender people, and authorities also hold people who cannot "satisfactorily account" for their presence. Outright International's overview reports torture and sexual violence in detention after the coup, and rights groups document arrest, torture and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities. Compulsory military service announced in February 2024 and the 2024 Conscription Law have driven queer people into fear and displacement.

Institutional recourse is effectively absent. The "Rainbow Amid the Storm" research found that 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and more than 68% fear repercussions from abusers. Violence by police against trans women is documented in individual cases: a trans woman describing a 2016 arrest recounted stripping, a beating and 14 days of detention after walking home at night while accused of sex work, and 2013 arrests in Mandalay saw trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, which police called a "public service."

Cultural control runs alongside the criminal law. In January 2025 the junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions against their publishers. Section 377 was in active use before the coup as well, illustrated by the 2018 charging of an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner over an allegation involving an employee.

Outright International's assessment, updated March 2026, is that trans and LGBT visitors should avoid Myanmar entirely.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation predates the coup and has been applied continuously: the 2018 sodomy charge against a prominent advocate and the 2013 and 2016 detentions of trans women show a pattern of enforcement that the post-2021 security environment has intensified rather than created.

Two sources give different kill counts for the same period, 17 recorded by the parallel government against 5 to 12 documented in a June 2024 UN submission, which reflects differing verification thresholds rather than a settled figure.

Penalties under Section 377 are reported inconsistently across sources, as life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and the exact sentencing range in current practice is not resolved by the available material.

Censorship of LGBTQ-themed publishing in 2025 indicates that the state's reach extends to representation and documentation, not only to conduct, which affects what material a visitor or researcher can obtain locally.

Visibility of gender-diverse people predates the current regime: nat kadaws, spirit mediums who are culturally visible transgender women, have long been part of public life, so visibility and criminalisation have coexisted for decades.
localsOnly:
Residents face the 2024 Conscription Law and the compulsory military service announced in February 2024, which the ASEAN SOGIE Caucus reports pushes queer people into fear and displacement, alongside the risk of call-up that applies to the general population.

The Organization Registration Law of October 2022 imposes prison terms on organisations that fail to comply with registration requirements, which constrains the civil-society groups and community organisations on which LGBT residents depend.

Community research indicates that half of LGBT respondents place no confidence in the legal system and more than 68% fear reprisal from those who abuse them, which shapes whether residents report violence at all.

Transgender residents are exposed to Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act on face covering, punishable by up to three months, and to arrest on suspicion of sex work, with documented stripping and beating in custody.

Nat kadaws remain a culturally established form of transgender visibility, holding social roles that persist despite the criminal law.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address legal gender recognition, marker or document changes, marriage or partner recognition, hate-crime provisions, or access to gender-affirming care in Myanmar; the current state of these questions is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory describes entry, visa or border-screening procedures as they affect trans travellers, so any screening risk at the point of entry is not sourced.

The treatment of LGBT people in areas outside military control is not covered by the inventory and remains unresolved; the resistance-controlled areas referenced in earlier framing are not substantiated by any source provided.

The precise penalty range under Section 377, and whether the 2018 charge against the advocate proceeded to conviction, are not resolved by the material supplied.

The scope of the two kill counts differs and neither source defines its verification method, so the true figure for LGBT deaths since February 2021 is not established.
